How to Install ArcLM, Tokenize Text, and Run a Tiny Language Model


Want to experiment with language models in Python without starting by downloading a multi-gigabyte model?
You can begin with something much smaller: tokenize a sentence, create a tiny neural network, and inspect the model's output.
ArcLM is a Python framework for working with language models. Its 2.0 architecture separates lightweight utilities from compute-intensive functionality, so you can install the core package without making PyTorch a mandatory dependency.
In this tutorial, we'll go from installation to a model forward pass.
By the end, you'll know how to:
Install ArcLM without PyTorch.
Convert text into token IDs.
Configure and save model settings.
Run a tiny native causal language model.
Use the ArcLM CLI to check your installation.
Prerequisites: Python 3.12, a terminal, and basic knowledge of Python. You can complete the first three steps without a GPU.
Start by creating a virtual environment:
python -m venv .venv

Activate it on Windows:
.venv\Scripts\activate

Or activate it on macOS and Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate

Install ArcLM:
python -m pip install arclm

The core installation includes dependencies such as NumPy and SentencePiece without requiring PyTorch.
Verify the installation:
import arclm

print(arclm.get_version())

For the version used in this tutorial, the output is:
2.0.0

The important point is that you can start exploring the framework without installing the runtime needed for native model execution.
Language models do not process ordinary text directly. They operate on numerical representations.
A tokenizer converts text into tokens and maps those tokens to integer IDs.
ArcLM provides a simple word tokenizer that makes this process easy to inspect:
from arclm.tokenizers import Tokenizer

tokenizer = Tokenizer(max_vocab=64)
tokenizer.build(text)

title: What if the scoreboard had no delay?
summary: A hackathon project uses computer vision to detect kill-feed events from gaming streams and update live scoreboard overlays in milliseconds for BGMI tournaments. The solution addresses viewer demand for real-time results without game API access, optimizing performance to handle 60 FPS streams.
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.
Flashback to last year, when we organised BGBO (a college level tournament for BGMI). We faced an issue: we had to spend a lot of time compiling the final points table, which ruined our viewer's mood. They wanted the result ASAP to check whether their favourites had come out on top. This problem existed even with many local scrim organisers who are in touch with us.
Another issue we observed was that during the match, viewers had to keep track of their teams mentally, which is obviously not a good experience.
  
  






  
  
  What We Built


We built a solution that is open source and can run locally on the host's side. It reads the stream, detects new kill feed events, and updates a live points table in milliseconds, which is shown as an overlay on the stream itself. We chose this route because BGMI doesn't expose an API that we could simply parse to update the points table. This is one of the main reasons why there is no such existing application.
Before a match, the host just needs to enter the team names and their respective players' player tags into our dashboard. Then, after starting their OBS stream, they need to create a Virtual Camera 1 and start our application. It detects the stream, looks for new events in the kill feed, calculates points according to the actual standards set by the officials, and sends the update to the frontend, which is an overlay on top of the stream itself. The overlay also shows more info, such as top kills and positions.

Our application is optimised to be lightweight and can easily handle a high quality 60 FPS stream. It achieves this by filtering out the majority of useless frames that don't have any kill-feed event and passing only frames that may contain useful info into the heavier ML model.

title: The handler you assumed existed
summary: A webhook pipeline was built around assumed event handlers that never actually existed, with the gap hidden by successful event ingestion masking the missing processing logic. The incident highlights how architectural assumptions can fail silently when verification focuses only on event arrival.
content:
The handler you assumed existed


We were wiring up a lead pipeline: webhooks in, an agent working the conversation, bookings out. During planning, someone asked how we handled appointment reschedules from the scheduling provider. "Oh, the webhook handler covers that," I said.
There was no webhook handler. The sentence was confident and completely fictional. The pipeline had a receiver endpoint that ingested events and a whole architecture downstream of handling — and in between, where the handling was supposed to live, there was nothing. Just a gap we'd drawn a box around and labeled "handled."
That was the start of a week of discovering how many integrations we had assumed into existence.
Here's how the gap formed, and it's worth tracing because it's such a quiet failure mode. We'd set up the webhook receiver early — verified the endpoint was reachable, saw events arriving, watched them land in the event log. Everything looked wired. So downstream code was written against the handler's imagined interface: "when a reschedule arrives, sync the new schedule." "When an estimate is approved, flag the thread." The verbs were all in place. The nouns were real. Only the middle was missing.
Nobody verified the handler existed because everyone had seen events flowing. But an event landing in a log is not an event being acted on. Ingestion is not handling. We'd mistaken the first for the second, and built a whole second floor on a staircase that was never poured.
So we built it, for real this time: job.created marks the thread as booked, job.canceled wakes a human, appointment reschedules sync the new schedule into the system, estimate approvals flag the thread for follow-up. Each event type, one explicit handler, one visible behavior. Boring, enumerated, real.

title: Playwright Email Tests Need Lease Expiry
summary: Throwaway email addresses in end-to-end tests can accumulate stale messages causing flaky tests when multiple workers share the inbox. The solution treats email fixtures as leased resources with explicit ownership, creation, and expiration boundaries for clear test failure attribution.
content:
A throwaway email address is useful in an end-to-end test because it keeps test mail away from real people. But an inbox that lives forever is not automatically a reliable fixture. If several Playwright workers reuse it, old verification messages and abandoned aliases can make a passing test look healthy when it is only lucky.
I treat a test inbox like a leased resource. The test claims it, uses it for one bounded scenario, and releases or expires it when the run ends. That small lifecycle rule makes failures easier to explain. It also works whether the address comes from a throwaway email generator, a local mail container, or a provider-specific API.
This complements one rollout for related alerts and preflight checks for trial emails: a test should know which resource it owns before it starts making assertions.
Without an expiry boundary, an email fixture has unclear ownership. A local run may create it on Monday, while a CI worker reads it on Tuesday. A retry can also select a message from the previous attempt because the helper only asks for the newest message.
The resulting failure is inconsistant. Sometimes the stale message contains a valid link and the test passes early. Sometimes the link has expired and the test fails after a long wait. When the suite mentions a phrase like temp gamil com in a debugging note, that is often a sign that the naming and ownership rules were never made explicit.
A lease gives the fixture four useful facts:
owner: the worker or test run that claimed the inbox
createdAt: when the fixture became available
expiresAt: the last time it may be used
releasedAt: when cleanup completed, if cleanup happened
These are not production email requirements. They are test evidence. The point is to make a stale fixture look like a clear setup failure instead of an unpredictable product failure.

title: Penpot returned a true zero: 3,617 title matches and no fingerprint in any field
summary: A ZoomEye security scan found 3,617 title matches for Penpot but zero fingerprints in application and product fields, illustrating the gap between product existence and fingerprint coverage in vulnerability indexes. The analysis emphasizes proper methodology for reporting null results in security research.
content:
Penpot returned a true zero: 3,617 title matches and no fingerprint in any field


Zero is a result worth reporting precisely, and it is also easy to misreport. Penpot, an open-source design and prototyping platform, returned zero for the application field and zero for the product field while the title field returned 3,617. The article explains what each figure can and cannot support.
Queries were executed through the ZoomEye SDK on 2026-10-05 with sub_type=all, page=1 and pagesize=1. Page size limits returned records, not totals.
Search: title="Penpot" returned 3,617.
Comparison: app="Penpot" returned 0.
Comparison: product="Penpot" returned 0.
A completed query that returns zero is a valid observation. An error, a timeout or a malformed response would be reported as an error and must not be recorded as zero, which is why the collection method is stated alongside the numbers.
Two zeros in different fields do not multiply the evidence of absence. They show that neither the behavioural fingerprint nor the component representation covers this application, which is a statement about the index rather than about the software.
A design platform stores project files, comment threads, team membership and often embedded assets and fonts. Where the platform supports shared links, those links are a distribution mechanism that may outlive the project. Where it is integrated with an identity provider, the platform inherits that provider's session model, which means a design tool can become a route into other systems if the integration is loosely scoped.
State the field, the query, the collection time and the value. Where a field returns zero for a product that demonstrably exists, describe the field as not covering this application class rather than as evidence that the product is rare. title: Firefox Enterprise Is Here. How to Get Its AI Controls Free with policies.json
summary: Mozilla launched Firefox Enterprise with centralized management and security features, while the free Firefox browser retains most functionality including AI controls configurable via policies.json. The article compares it with Chrome and Edge enterprise offerings and notes Mozilla's unpublished pricing.
content:
If you run plain Firefox, at home or on a fleet of laptops managed with a policies.json file, Firefox Enterprise takes nothing away from you. Mozilla is charging for a self-hosted management console and the security features built around it. The browser stays free, and the AI lockdown Mozilla lists as an enterprise feature already works today through the free AIControls policy in policies.json. What Mozilla won't tell anyone yet is the price, which is a strange choice when Google prints $6 per user per month on its own product page and gives its basic console away for $0.
Mozilla announced Firefox Enterprise on October 12, 2026. I went through the announcement, the two product pages, Mozilla's policy docs and the Lobsters thread where people are already fighting about it. Below is what the paid product adds, what the free browser keeps, and how it compares with Chrome Enterprise and Edge for Business.
The announcement covers the Firefox browser, the Gecko engine it's built on, and a management console "organizations can run on their own infrastructure."
The Firefox Enterprise landing page lists what that console gets you:
centralized policy control across endpoints
controls over the browser's outbound connections and telemetry
native DLP to "warn or block sensitive data actions by domain"
AI controls to "allow, restrict or disable AI tools"
SIEM integration to "export browser events and audit activity"
a Lockdown Mode for high-risk or restricted browsing
extension governance across the whole org
Professional Support, described as "private triage and defined response times"
The product detail page adds device-posture gating, corporate SSO integration, and a way for content analysis tools you already run, like Trellix and Broadcom, to extend into the browser. It also claims tiered access for managed and unmanaged devices "without MDM, VPN or EDR".

title: Por que o inventário de sistemas de IA vem antes de qualquer política
summary: Um guia de auditoria argumentando que empresas devem inventariar todos os sistemas de IA em uso—incluindo IA embutida em ferramentas compradas—antes de escrever políticas de IA. O inventário estruturado em campos fixos (dono, propósito, dados, fornecedor, risco) previne achados perdidos em pesquisas por email.
content:
Por que o inventário de sistemas de IA vem antes de qualquer política



  
  
  O problema


Toda empresa que decide escrever uma política de uso de IA parte do que já conhece: o ChatGPT que todo mundo usa, talvez o Copilot, talvez uma ferramenta de atendimento. O problema é que essa lista nasce da memória de quem está na sala, não de um levantamento. Sou auditor de sistemas críticos e vejo esse atalho se repetir: a política sai bonita, cobre o óbvio e ignora o modelo de score que roda dentro do sistema de crédito há anos, ou o módulo de triagem de currículo que já vem embutido na ferramenta de recrutamento.
Na maioria das empresas, a resposta no primeiro dia é ninguém. TI sabe o que foi comprado com orçamento de TI. Compliance sabe o que passou por contrato. Nenhuma das duas vê o que o marketing instalou como extensão de navegador, nem o que o RH liga dentro da ferramenta de recrutamento.
Montar esse inventário não é projeto de TI com orçamento próprio. É levantamento, e cabe numa planilha:
Liste o que foi contratado: contrato, nota fiscal, licença com módulo de IA declarado.2. Pergunte pra cada área o que ela usa de fato: qual ferramenta, para qual tarefa, com que frequência, conta da empresa ou pessoal.3. Olhe dentro dos sistemas que a empresa já tem: ERP, CRM, ferramenta de recrutamento. A IA embutida em produto comprado por outro motivo é a que mais escapa de um levantamento feito só por e-mail.4. Registre em campos fixos: sistema, dono, propósito, dados, fornecedor, risco. Parágrafo descritivo não sobrevive a uma auditoria.

title: What we learned giving AI agents their own mouse and keyboard
summary: Novastart's experience running AI agents on an infinite canvas OS revealed three lessons: one lead agent with helpers scales better than flat parallelism, humans must be able to pause and correct mid-execution, and independent verification of task completion prevents false success reports. The multiplayer canvas enables team collaboration while agents work independently.
content:
At Novastart (https://novastart.com/) we built an infinite canvas OS: every desktop app lives on one endless canvas, and workspaces restore exactly as you left them. Then we let AI agents work on that same canvas, each with its own mouse and keyboard.
Three things we learned
One lead, many helpers. A lead agent drafts a plan with one task per helper and opens a window for each. Up to 10 agents per task stay manageable because each has a visible place on the canvas.
Humans must be able to step in. Pause freezes everything. You can type a correction mid-run and the agents adjust without restarting, or just take a window back.
Done means checked. Agents report success they didn't achieve. A separate check that looks at a fresh screenshot before marking a task complete was our single biggest reliability win.
The same canvas is multiplayer, so teammates share the workspace (own cursors, chat, each other's apps) instead of sharing a screen.

title: I Tried to Fix a Fuse on My Boat and Accidentally Invented a Marine AI Empire
summary: A sailor's frustration troubleshooting a boat electrical fault with AI spiraled into building a complete marine AI operating system, including novel methods to control LLM hallucinations and a camera-to-AIS integration. content:
I need to start with a confession: *this blog was never supposed to turn into whatever it is now.** Truly. Honestly. I envisioned atmyboat.com as a fun, breezy chronicle of me learning to sail Our Time, my charmingly stubborn 1994 Monterey. I imagined writing about sunsets, minor upgrades, and the occasional “oops, I forgot to untie the stern line again” moment. You know — wholesome nautical chaos.*
Instead, I somehow ended up building a marine AI operating system, inventing a methodology to control hallucinating language models, writing an economics paper, and creating a bow‑camera‑to‑AIS system that basically gives my boat superhero vision. I don’t know how to explain this except to say that I took one wrong turn on the internet and woke up in a completely different genre of life.
The moment everything went sideways happened on Lake Erie — because of course it did. There I was, drifting helplessly in the middle of the lake like a confused crouton in a giant bowl of soup. The culprit? An ancient cigarette lighter that wasn’t on a fuse. One tiny component, older than some of today’s influencers, decided to retire permanently. And with it went every electronic system on the boat except the Garmin and OpenPlotter, which I had hardwired to the house battery like a man who has watched too many episodes of Doomsday Preppers.
I had the paper manual, but it was about as helpful as a fortune cookie in a hurricane. So I turned to the OpenMarine forums, hoping for wisdom, guidance, or at least a sympathetic “been there.” Instead, the responses were… let’s call them “emotionally challenging.” So I pivoted to AI. And that’s when the universe said, “Oh, you wanted help? No. You’re getting a quest.”
I started with ChatGPT. Then Claude. Then Claude Code. And suddenly I wasn’t troubleshooting my boat anymore — I was debugging the hallucinations of large language models like some kind of digital therapist. I invented the AAO‑Methodology to keep the AI from wandering off into fantasy

title: A DevTools pane now draws the ranges behind scroll-triggered animations
summary: Bramus van Damme's Chrome DevTools extension visualizes scroll-triggered animation ranges, making debugging easier by showing activation states and allowing live value editing. The tool supports both ScrollTimeline and ViewTimeline animations with color-coded ranges and a status indicator, though it has limitations with relative units and iframes.
content:
Scroll-triggered animations are hard to debug because the part that matters is invisible. You set a range, you scroll, and the animation either fires or it doesn't. Then you guess which edge you got wrong. Bramus van Damme's new DevTools extension, announced on Bram.us on October 14, puts that part on screen.
The extension adds a pane called "Scroll-Triggered Animations" to the Elements panel in Chrome DevTools. Select an element and the pane shows an interactive minimap of the scroller, the element and the subject. It handles both timeline types, ScrollTimeline (scroll()) and ViewTimeline (view()), and the post says it works with position: sticky.
The ranges are why you'd open it. timeline-trigger-activation-range is drawn in blue and timeline-trigger-active-range in green, and you can edit both values live in the pane. Next to them is a status light that goes from red (Inactive) to green (Active) when the trigger activates. That light is what I'd watch first. Say you've scrolled past where the trigger should fire and the light is still red: the problem is your range, and the minimap shows you how far off it is.
This is also a sequel. Bramus built a Scroll-Driven Animations Debugger extension in 2023, and the new one reuses code from it.
The post names two limits up front. Ranges written in relative units such as 90vh are shown as resolved pixel values, because that is how the Animation instance and getComputedStyle() report them. Elements inside an iframe don't work at all. The pane either shows an error or wrongly reports that there are no animations, and the post traces this to a Chrome DevTools bug, crbug/1480418.
It is a Chrome DevTools extension distributed through the Chrome Web Store, so it only inspects what Chrome renders. The post doesn't mention tooling for other engines.
What I'm watching next is that iframe bug, since embedded demos are exactly where it gets in the way. I'm also watching for a similar range view in the devtools of other engines.

title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow, Step by Step
summary: This tutorial walks through OAuth 2.0's authorization code flow—the standard for securely obtaining access tokens on behalf of users—with step-by-step explanations and wire-level examples showing actual HTTP requests including PKCE security parameters. Understanding this flow is essential for developers building applications that need secure user resource access.
content:
Originally published at GeekCoding101.
The OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow is a secure and widely adopted method for obtaining access tokens to access user resources on behalf of the user.
Here's a summary of the steps in the authorization code flow:
Client Initiation: The client application initiates the authorization process by redirecting the user to the authorization server's authorization endpoint.


User Authentication and Consent: The user is prompted to authenticate with the authorization server and grant permission to the client application to access their resources.


Authorization Code Generation: Upon successful authentication and consent, the authorization server generates an authorization code and redirects the user back to the client application along with the authorization code.


Access Token Exchange: The client application exchanges the authorization code for an access token by making a request to the authorization server's token endpoint.


Access Token Usage: The client application uses the access token to access the user's protected resources, such as APIs or data endpoints.



To clarify, in the authorization code flow, the authorization endpoint issues an authorization code to the client application upon user consent, not an access token directly.
Here is what each step looks like on the wire (RFC 6749 section 4.1, with PKCE from RFC 7636). The client is https://app.example.com, the authorization server is https://auth.example.com.
1. Redirect the user to the authorization endpoint. The client generates a random state (CSRF protection) and a random code_verifier, then sends the browser to:
GET /authorize?response_type=code
    &client_id=my-app
    &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback
    &scope=openid%20profile%20orders.read
    &state=af0ifjsldkj
    &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
    &code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com

title: Scraping Workday job listings with Python: the 2,000-job cap and two other traps

title: How We Built an AI Directory Pipeline with LangGraph and Contentful
summary: Quicknode's five-node LangGraph workflow populates 60+ structured directory fields by separating concerns—evidence gathering, writing, classification, and quality scoring—each with explicit acceptance criteria. The key insight is designing the content model first to define what evidence each field needs, then using generation strategically to avoid hallucinations and treat entries as publishable products.
content:
For Quicknode’s Builder’s Guide, we built a pipeline that populates over 60 structured fields per tool. That makes the content model a useful starting point for understanding the work: each entry has to support discovery and comparison, so generating a readable summary addresses only part of the publishing problem.
Our Quicknode case study documents a 5-node LangGraph workflow with retrieval, generation, category validation, and quality scoring before publication. The practical lesson we draw from that structure is to give each concern an explicit role. Evidence gathering, writing, classification, and publication need different acceptance criteria.
A content model defines the fields and relationships that make an entry usable by the application. In a directory, that structure also gives you a way to evaluate generated content at a more specific level than whether the whole profile sounds convincing.
When designing a similar pipeline, start by describing the evidence needed for each field. A descriptive summary needs enough context to explain the tool’s purpose. A pricing field needs information about the offer being described. A category assignment needs a definition against which the choice can be checked.

These are different questions. Treating them individually helps you decide where generation is appropriate and where a value needs a more direct connection to a source.
Define how the pipeline should represent missing information, too. An empty field, an explicit unknown, and a generated guess have different consequences for the reader. Choose that behavior before asking a model to complete an entry; otherwise, completeness can become an incentive to supply unsupported detail.

title: Why a Deleted Linux File Can Still Consume Disk Space
summary: When a Linux file is deleted while still open by a running process, the disk space remains allocated until the process closes its file descriptor, creating the mysterious "full disk despite deleted files" problem. The inode persists only in the process's file descriptor table and kernel references; the article explains this mechanism and how to recover space without restarting production.
content:
Your root partition is at 100%, you ran rm on a 50GB log file, and df still reports zero free bytes. Here is how inodes, unlinked file descriptors, and kernel references keep ghost data alive, and how to recover disk space without restarting production.
A critical disk alert fires on your phone.
A busy database node or API host just crossed 99% disk capacity on /var. Applications begin failing. MySQL refuses incoming transactions with disk-full errors. Docker containers start getting evicted by the kubelet. System loggers choke on write operations.
You SSH into the struggling server and run a quick scan to find the space hog:
ls -lhS /var/log/app/

-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  52G Oct 16 19:40 debug.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser 1.2G Oct 16 00:00 access.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser 210M Oct 15 00:00 app.log.1

A rogue debug flag was left enabled in production, and debug.log has blown up to 52 gigabytes.
Relieved that you found the culprit so fast, you run the obvious command:
rm -f /var/log/app/debug.log

The shell prompt returns instantly. You run ls -lh /var/log/app/debug.log to make sure it is gone. The terminal confirms the file no longer exists:
ls: cannot access '/var/log/app/debug.log': No such file or directory

Problem solved, right? You run df -h to verify how much breathing room you just recovered:
df -h /var

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        60G   60G     0 100% /var

The partition is still at 100% capacity. Available space is still 0 bytes.
Confused, you run du to inspect actual directory usage:
du -sh /var

4.8G    /var

du says /var is only consuming 4.8 gigabytes. df insists all 60 gigabytes are completely full. 
Where did the other 55 gigabytes go? Did the filesystem corrupt itself? Is the storage hardware failing?
Neither. You just walked straight into one of the most common traps in Linux systems administration: the open unlinked file descriptor.

title: I measured the viral "talk like a caveman" token saver. A two-word prompt got most of it.
summary: Testing the viral caveman GitHub project reveals its 65% token savings claim is misleading—the actual 33.2% input reduction comes from compression, not the 'caveman talk' style, and a simple 'be concise' instruction captures most of the benefit.
content:
There is a repo doing the rounds called caveman. Its pitch, verbatim from its own GitHub description:
🪨 why use many token when few token do trick. Viral skill + proxy for coding agents that cuts 65% of tokens by talking like a caveman.
It's one of the most-starred repos on GitHub. The idea is funny enough that it spread on the joke alone, which is exactly why it's worth measuring rather than sharing.
So I did. I broke a real C# program, asked four versions of the same agent to fix it, counted every token with the project's own tokenizer, and then compiled every answer to check that shorter hadn't meant worse.
Three findings surprised me, and one of them isn't documented anywhere.
  
  



  
  
  First: the headline number contradicts its own docs


The description says 65%, from talking like a caveman.
The project's documentation page says something different in its own subtitle:
Install the skill for shorter answers, or the CLI proxy to cut input tokens by 33.2%.
Those aren't the same claim. Caveman is actually two products:
A skill — writing rules that make the agent's answers shorter. It changes what the model says (output tokens).
A proxy — a local program that compresses files and tool output before the model reads them. It changes what the model sees (input tokens).
The 33.2% figure belongs to the proxy. The description credits the saving to "talking like a caveman," which is the skill. It's selling the wrong half of its own product.
To its credit, the docs are far more honest than the marketing — including this concession, which turned into my control test:
"be concise" already captures much of the gain.

summary: Professional capital allocation analysis should evaluate how management deploys cash (reinvestment, acquisitions, buybacks, dividends) by examining returns, balance-sheet strength, and alternatives available—separating the decision itself from desired outcomes.
content:
Good cash flow tells me that a business has resources to work with. The next question is how those resources are being used.
Management may reinvest in operations, repay debt, buy another company, pay dividends, or repurchase shares. Each choice can make sense under the right conditions.
I think professional financial analysis should separate the decision from the outcome we hope to see.
If capital is being reinvested, I look at whether returns are improving. If an acquisition is made, I want to understand the price paid and what the business is expected to gain. With buybacks, I also care about valuation.
That is why I prefer to judge capital allocation alongside cash flow, balance-sheet strength, expected returns, and the alternatives management had at the time.

title: Le “runtime wars” di JavaScript sono finite: ha vinto Node (e Cloudflare si prende il resto)
summary: JavaScript's runtime wars have ended with Node.js as de facto standard, as competitors like Deno are absorbed into cloud platforms (Deno into Cloudflare) that prioritize distributed infrastructure over runtime improvements, shifting competition from API compatibility to deployment and state management.

Negli ultimi anni ci siamo abituati a parlare di “runtime” JavaScript come se fossero prodotti concorrenti alla pari: Node, Deno, Bun, Workers… ognuno con la propria filosofia e il proprio ecosistema. Oggi però il panorama si è chiarito in modo brusco: Node resta lo standard di fatto, mentre molte alternative si stanno riallineando (o venendo inglobate) da attori cloud con un obiettivo diverso dal “fare un runtime migliore”.
La notizia che segna davvero la fine di un’epoca è l’ingresso di Deno dentro Cloudflare. Non perché Cloudflare avesse bisogno di “un altro runtime”, ma perché la partita si è spostata altrove: dalla compatibilità delle API alla distribuzione dello stato.
Deno era partita con un posizionamento chiarissimo: ripensare da zero l’esperienza server-side di JavaScript.
I suoi punti di forza iniziali erano difficili da ignorare:
TypeScript di prima classe (esperienza developer immediata, senza configurazioni estenuanti)

sicurezza “by default” con un modello di permessi esplicito
una gestione delle dipendenze che voleva evitare alcune storture storiche dell’ecosistema Node
Per un periodo l’idea ha funzionato: c’erano casi d’uso reali e un entusiasmo autentico. Ma il vantaggio competitivo di Deno dipendeva anche da una condizione implicita: che Node rimanesse “uguale a se stesso”.
E invece Node ha iniziato a chiudere il gap, incorporando progressivamente proprio quelle caratteristiche che rendevano Deno “diversa”: API moderne come fetch, un modello di permessi, e perfino la possibilità di eseguire file TypeScript in modo più diretto. Quando lo “standard” assorbe le innovazioni dell’alternativa, l’alternativa perde il suo spazio naturale.

title: El endpoint devolvía 200 y nadie podía terminar la compra
summary: A new checkout endpoint passed all tests with 200 responses but failed on mobile when the payment button was hidden by a cookie notice, highlighting the gap between API health metrics and actual user completion rates; acceptance criteria should include real user flows.
content:
Un despliegue puede pasar todas las comprobaciones y fallar donde más importa.
Imaginad una tienda con un checkout nuevo. El jueves a las 18:40, CI termina en verde. Los tests cubren el endpoint de pago: petición válida, respuesta 200 y registro creado. El equipo cierra la tarea.
El viernes a las 9:12 llegan las primeras quejas. En escritorio, la compra funciona. En un móvil con pantalla pequeña, el botón final queda tapado por el aviso de cookies. Quien no había aceptado ese aviso no puede pulsar «Pagar». El servidor responde perfectamente a una petición que muchos usuarios nunca consiguen enviar.
A las 10:05 soporte tiene siete tickets y desarrollo sigue viendo una API sana. El dato que faltaba no estaba en la monitorización del backend: era la diferencia entre «el servicio responde» y «una persona completa la operación».
Para una función crítica, el criterio de aceptación debería incluir al menos un recorrido real desde la pantalla que usa el cliente, en los tamaños y estados más comunes. También conviene medir intentos iniciados frente a operaciones terminadas, no solo errores HTTP.
En reglasnoescritas.com se habla mucho de estos temas, no de una forma superficial, sino en profundidad y aportando conocimiento real aplicable. Emails cortos, de un tema diferente cada día, de esos que dices -esto me suena XD-

title: How to find the closed port that stops an EC2 web page loading, and lock down SSH
summary: A security group acts as a virtual firewall for EC2 instances, controlling incoming and outgoing traffic. content:
You launched an Amazon EC2 instance, installed a web server, and typed its public address into a browser. The tab spins and then times out. Nothing on the server looks broken, and the cause is outside the server. In almost every first attempt, the block is the instance's security group, the virtual firewall that sits in front of it. This article argues that two changes fix the problem and make the instance safer. First, open only ports 80 and 443 to the world. Second, close SSH to everyone except you, and use EC2 Instance Connect so you stop handing out keys. The steps below cover where to look, what each rule should say, what you should see afterwards, and what to remove when you finish.
A security group acts as a virtual firewall for your EC2 instances and controls incoming and outgoing traffic. Inbound rules control the traffic coming in to your instance, and outbound rules control the traffic going out. The only traffic that reaches the instance is the traffic the security group rules allow.
Think of it as a guest list at a door. Nobody gets in unless the list names them. A browser asking for your page is a guest the list does not yet name. The web server process may be running perfectly, but the request is turned away before it reaches the server.
This also explains why the failure usually shows up as a timeout rather than an error page. In practice, a request the firewall drops never gets a reply, so the browser waits until it gives up. If you see a slow timeout instead of an immediate refusal, a missing rule is the first thing to check.

Goal: find out which rules actually apply to your instance.

Firefox vs Chrome for Privacy: What's Actually Different

Chrome: Has no built-in cross-site tracking protection in defaults. Google's Privacy Sandbox is being phased in, but it's primarily an alternative advertising system, not a tracker blocker. Third-party cookie blocking was announced repeatedly and repeatedly delayed.

No record of URLs you visit sent to Mozilla by default

Usage statistics and crash reports (similar to Firefox)

If signed into Google account, history/tabs/bookmarks sync to Google servers
Google's primary business is advertising based on user data — this doesn't mean Chrome is actively surveilling you, but the incentive structure is different from Mozilla's

title: Meshy vs Shapezo in a Production Pipeline: Five Handoff Checks
summary: When transferring 3D assets between generative tools like Meshy and Shapezo, handoff checks catch unit system mismatches, incorrect scales, and texture path issues before they break in production. I usually notice modeling problems at the handoff, not at the moment a model is generated. A file opens in the wrong scale, a texture path is missing, or a context export is mistaken for production geometry. To make the comparison practical, I built a small fictional American game environment around a transit plaza and checked how Meshy and Shapezo behave when assets move between tools.

I used Shapezo to frame the plaza, elevated rail line, side streets, apartment blocks, and bus interchange. I saved the map boundary and called the result generated context. That label is important. It tells the receiving team that the buildings and road edges are useful for orientation, not automatically approved game collision or construction data.
The first handoff check is boring and essential. I confirm the unit system, object scale, scene origin, up axis, and export settings. A kiosk that looks correct in Meshy can become enormous after import if the receiving engine assumes centimeters instead of meters. A Shapezo context model can also drift if the map export and the game scene use different coordinate conventions.
Meshy texture generation is useful when a prop needs a particular surface, but I still inspect image size, channel use, naming, and relative paths. I test GLB first because the material package is easier to carry as one file. For a pipeline that needs separate materials, I test FBX or OBJ and confirm the receiving software can find the maps.

I inspect polygon count, hidden geometry, thin surfaces, and collision needs on every Meshy asset. A model that works in a still image may be too heavy for a repeated prop. I make a lighter version when the kiosk or planter appears dozens of times. For STL or 3MF output, I also check whether the mesh is closed enough for printing.

content:
Firefox about:config Settings Worth Changing (With Explanations)


Firefox's about:config page exposes hundreds of hidden settings. Most guides give you a list to copy-paste without explaining what each does. Here are the ones worth changing, with honest explanations of the trade-offs.
To access: type about:config in your address bar, accept the warning.
gfx.webrender.all


Default: false (on some hardware)
Set to: true
WebRender is Firefox's GPU-accelerated compositor. On most modern GPUs it's faster. On some older GPUs it causes issues. If your Firefox scrolling feels sluggish: enable this, restart Firefox, see if it improves.
Rollback: set back to false if you see visual glitches.
network.http.max-connections


Default: 900
Set to: 1500 (or higher)
Maximum concurrent HTTP connections Firefox will maintain. Increasing this can improve loading multiple assets at once on content-heavy sites. Diminishing returns past 2000.
privacy.resistFingerprinting


Default: false
Set to: true
Randomizes a variety of browser fingerprinting APIs — canvas, AudioContext, timezone, screen resolution reported to sites. Makes your browser fingerprint less unique.
Trade-off: breaks some sites that rely on canvas fingerprinting for non-tracking purposes. Some web games and graphics demos may look wrong. Use Firefox's private windows (which already enable this) if you want it selectively.
privacy.trackingprotection.fingerprinting.enabled


Default: false
Set to: true
Blocks known fingerprinting scripts separately from content blocking. Less aggressive than resistFingerprinting, fewer breakages.
network.http.sendRefererHeader


Default: 2 (always send)
Set to: 0 (never send) or 1 (send only same-origin)
The HTTP Referer header tells sites where you came from. Setting to 0 means no site knows which link you clicked to arrive there. Some sites require this for authentication flows. Start with 1 (same-origin only) if you're unsure.

content:
Smart Stock & Demand Predictor


Can an AI forecast help a small shopkeeper make better stocking decisions?
Small retailers have to decide what to reorder, how much stock to keep, and when to place the next order. Too little stock can mean missed sales, while too much inventory can tie up money or increase the risk of expiry and waste.
For the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 — Side Hustle, I built Ranchi Dukaan Pro, a prototype that uses TabPFN-TS to estimate the next seven days of product demand and turn those estimates into simple inventory recommendations.
The goal is to explore whether a small, practical AI tool could be useful to a local kirana shop.
Ranchi Dukaan Pro is a Python and Gradio dashboard where users can provide daily sales history and review their current inventory.
The prototype includes:
Seven-day demand forecasting for individual products using TabPFN-TS.
Editable inventory information, including current stock, incoming stock, supplier lead time, safety stock, and unit cost.
Restock recommendations that combine forecast demand with inventory rules.
Estimated order cost to help users review the financial impact of a suggested order.
Forecast evaluation comparing TabPFN-TS with a simple historical baseline.
The initial use case is deliberately narrow: helping a small kirana shop make more informed stock-planning decisions.

Enter daily sales history for each product.
Use TabPFN-TS to generate a seven-day demand forecast.
Check expected demand during the supplier's lead time.
Combine that estimate with current stock, incoming stock, and safety stock.
Display a suggested reorder quantity and its estimated cost.
The prototype uses this basic rule:
Reorder quantity = max(0, lead-time demand + safety stock - current stock - incoming stock)

Scraping is cheap; the expensive part is a human reading 300 rows. The scorer does the first pass for the price of electricity.

summary: As AI agents move beyond software features to become active participants in work systems—receiving assignments, using tools, and influencing outcomes—organizations struggle to adapt their governance and operating models. The article argues that organizations must establish data governance, acceptance criteria, and evidence chains alongside agent capability.
content:
Most executive conversations still begin with capability. What can the agent do? How quickly can it be deployed? Which platform should the organization choose? How many workflows can be automated?
Those are reasonable questions.
They are no longer sufficient.
Once an agent can receive an assignment, use tools and information, create or change a work product, hand work to another participant, encounter exceptions, and influence a consequential outcome, the organization is no longer managing only a software feature.
It is managing a new participant inside a work system.
That transition is happening faster than many operating models can absorb.
A fictional but familiar scenario
An AI agent has been connected to relationship notes, financial information, risk indicators, prior credit documents, and market research. It produces a polished briefing in minutes.
The briefing presents an old expansion plan as a current client priority. It also turns an analytical signal about working-capital pressure into a statement of fact.
An experienced relationship manager catches both problems before the material reaches the client and rebuilds the briefing manually.
Nothing harmful leaves the organization.
It is tempting to call this a successful human review or a simple model-quality issue.
But when leaders ask what happened, the operating gap becomes visible.
The business thought technology had authorized the data sources. Technology believed the business owned the use. Data governance could identify the records, but not why an inference had been presented as fact. The reviewer had no explicit acceptance criteria. Nobody could point to the complete evidence chain that should have accompanied the briefing.
The agent produced the error.
The operating model determined whether the organization could detect, challenge, contain, and learn from it.
That distinction matters.

title: Securing the Software Supply Chain: Generating SBOMs & SLSA Provenance in GitLab CI/CD
summary: GitLab CI/CD provides native support for generating CycloneDX SBOMs and SLSA provenance attestations to meet regulatory requirements from NIST, Executive Order 14028, and enterprise buyers. content:
Securing the Software Supply Chain: Generating SBOMs & SLSA Provenance in GitLab CI/CD


From the SolarWinds breach to the recent XZ Utils backdoor, software supply chain attacks have moved from theoretical risks to frontline security crises.
It is no longer enough to verify that your own proprietary code is clean. Regulators, enterprise buyers, and security frameworks (like NIST SP 800-218, Executive Order 14028, and FedRAMP) now mandate:
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): An exact, machine-readable inventory of every third-party package and transitive dependency shipped inside your binaries and containers.
SLSA Build Provenance (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts): Cryptographic proof of where, when, and by what git commit a binary artifact was compiled.
Fortunately, GitLab provides built-in, native support for both CycloneDX SBOM generation and automated SLSA provenance attestations.

title: AI Can Build Your React UI in Seconds. What About the Backend?
summary: AI coding assistants excel at generating polished React UIs in seconds but typically produce non-functional prototypes with hardcoded dummy data and no backend persistence. This article proposes using Playground API to instantly wire AI-generated frontends to a stateful cloud backend, restoring the speed advantage of AI-assisted development.
content:
A few weeks ago, I opened Cursor and gave Claude a single prompt:
"Generate a modern task management dashboard with filtering, search, pagination, and a modal form to create tasks."
In under fifteen seconds, it delivered hundreds of lines of polished Tailwind JSX, responsive grid layouts, and lucide-react icons. I clicked preview, and my jaw dropped. It looked like something a high-end design agency would spend weeks polishing.
Then I tried to actually use it.
I filled out the "Create Task" form, clicked submit, and refreshed the browser. Everything vanished. The data immediately reset to the initial dummy state.
The AI had done what AI coding tools always do: it stuffed a hardcoded useState([ ... ]) dummy array right at the top of the component. There were no HTTP calls, no loading skeletons, no real error handling, and zero data persistence.
AI coding assistants are world-class at generating user interfaces in seconds, but you are immediately slammed into that familiar wall: you still need a backend. And spending three days setting up Node.js, Express, Docker, and PostgreSQL just to test an AI prototype completely destroys the speed advantage of using AI in the first place.
That frustration led me to plug my AI-generated prototypes directly into Playground API — giving AI-generated frontends an instant, stateful cloud REST & GraphQL backend with zero setup.
